blocks.text: Scenario A — Focused history
A 62-year-old woman presents with vaginal bleeding three years after menopause. Take a focused history and discuss your differential diagnoses.
Scenario B — Investigation interpretation
Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 12 mm in a woman with postmenopausal bleeding. Interpret the finding and explain the next step.
Scenario C — Counselling
An endometrial biopsy has confirmed endometrioid adenocarcinoma. Explain the diagnosis and the investigations required.
Scenario D — Management
A 58-year-old woman is diagnosed with endometrial cancer. Discuss staging and treatment options.
Scenario E — Viva
Explain the relationship between obesity, unopposed oestrogen and endometrial cancer.
Endometrial cancer is a malignant tumour arising from the endometrium, the inner lining of the uterus.
It is the most common type of uterine cancer in many countries and frequently presents with abnormal uterine bleeding, particularly postmenopausal bleeding.
1. Endometrioid carcinoma
The most common histological type.
Often associated with obesity, chronic anovulation and prolonged oestrogen exposure without adequate progesterone opposition.
2. Serous carcinoma
A high-grade histological type that may behave aggressively and can spread beyond the uterus even when the primary lesion appears relatively small.
3. Clear cell carcinoma and other uncommon types
Less common histologies that require specialist pathological classification because prognosis and treatment may differ.
Carcinosarcoma is another important aggressive uterine malignancy, classified as a high-grade carcinoma rather than a conventional pure sarcoma.

blocks.title: Endometrial cancers have historically been divided into two broad groups:

items.text: Type I: typically endometrioid, often oestrogen-associated and frequently lower grade.
Type II: traditionally includes serous and clear cell carcinomas, which are often more aggressive.

blocks.text: This is a useful teaching framework, but modern classification also uses molecular features, including mismatch repair status, POLE mutations and p53 abnormalities.

items.text: Chronic anovulation, including polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
Prolonged exposure to oestrogen without adequate progesterone opposition.
Nulliparity and infertility in some clinical contexts.
Lynch syndrome and other relevant inherited cancer predispositions.

blocks.text: These factors alter risk but do not mean that a woman with one or more of them necessarily has cancer.

content_groups.group_title: B. The role of unopposed oestrogen

blocks.text: Prolonged oestrogen stimulation without adequate progesterone opposition
Endometrial proliferation and possible hyperplasia
Accumulation of cellular and molecular abnormalities
Development of endometrioid carcinoma in a subset of patients

Adipose tissue contains aromatase, which converts androgens to oestrogens. Obesity can also contribute to insulin resistance and metabolic disturbances. These mechanisms are associated with increased risk of endometrial cancer.
Lynch syndrome is an inherited cancer predisposition associated with pathogenic variants in DNA mismatch repair genes. It increases the risk of endometrial and colorectal cancers, among others.
Consider genetic counselling or specialist assessment when personal and family history suggests an inherited cancer syndrome.

items.text: Heavy or irregular menstrual bleeding in perimenopausal women.

blocks.text: OSCE pearl: postmenopausal bleeding is the classic presenting symptom. Even a small amount of bleeding after menopause requires appropriate assessment.

items.text: Explain the purpose of the consultation.
Ensure privacy and use sensitive, non-judgmental language.

blocks.text: Example opening:

"I understand you have experienced vaginal bleeding after menopause. I would like to ask some questions about the bleeding, your previous menstrual history, medications and general health to determine the possible causes and appropriate investigations."

items.text: Is it spotting, moderate bleeding or heavy bleeding?
Has she used any medication or hormone therapy?
Use of hormonal contraception or menopausal hormone therapy.
Lynch syndrome or a relevant family history of endometrial and colorectal cancer.

blocks.text: Anticoagulants may worsen bleeding, but they do not remove the need to investigate its cause.

items.text: Heavy ongoing bleeding with haemodynamic compromise.
Severe pelvic pain or suspected sepsis.
A pelvic mass or findings concerning for advanced malignancy.
Urinary obstruction or other evidence of advanced disease.
Pulse, blood pressure, temperature and respiratory rate.
Body mass index and nutritional status.
Peripheral lymph nodes if clinically indicated.

blocks.text: With consent and a chaperone, examine the external genitalia and perform speculum examination as appropriate.

items.text: Blood emerging from the cervical os.

blocks.text: Bimanual examination may help assess uterine size, mobility, tenderness and adnexal masses.
A normal pelvic examination does not exclude endometrial cancer.
The objectives are to investigate the bleeding, obtain a histological diagnosis when indicated, assess tumour extent and determine the appropriate treatment.
TVUS is a common initial investigation for postmenopausal bleeding in appropriate patients.

For a woman with postmenopausal bleeding, a clearly visualised endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less is associated with a very low probability of endometrial cancer and may be reassuring after an initial episode in an appropriate clinical setting.
An endometrium thicker than 4 mm generally warrants endometrial sampling or further assessment.
However, persistent or recurrent bleeding requires further evaluation even when the endometrium is thin, particularly if the initial investigations are inconclusive or risk remains.
These thresholds apply to the appropriate postmenopausal bleeding context; they should not be applied indiscriminately to premenopausal women.
Endometrial sampling provides tissue for histopathology.
It may be performed using an outpatient sampling device, depending on the patient and local practice.
An inadequate or benign sample does not necessarily end the investigation when bleeding persists or clinical suspicion remains high.
Hysteroscopy allows direct visualisation of the uterine cavity and targeted biopsy of suspicious lesions.

items.text: Bleeding persists despite reassuring initial results.
Further assessment of the uterine cavity is required.
Renal and liver function where indicated.
Pelvic MRI for selected local staging questions.
CT or PET-CT when indicated to assess nodal or distant disease.
Molecular and immunohistochemical testing of tumour tissue as appropriate.

blocks.text: Once endometrial cancer is confirmed, the pathology report should establish the tumour type and grade, and the specialist team may request molecular testing.

items.text: POLE-mutated: often associated with a favourable prognosis.
Mismatch repair-deficient (MMRd): may prompt evaluation for Lynch syndrome, depending on the findings and clinical context.
p53-abnormal: commonly associated with more aggressive tumour biology.
No specific molecular profile (NSMP): a group without the defining features of the other categories.

blocks.text: Molecular classification contributes to modern risk stratification and may affect adjuvant treatment decisions.

Endometrial cancer is staged surgically and pathologically in many cases, with imaging and molecular information also contributing to treatment planning. The FIGO staging system was revised in 2023, so follow the version used by your training programme.
A simplified framework is:

rows: Disease confined to the uterine corpus, with specified subdivisions based on invasion and tumour characteristics
Cervical stromal involvement and/or other stage-defining adverse features under the applicable FIGO system
Local or regional spread beyond the uterus, including selected adnexal, vaginal, parametrial or nodal involvement
Invasion of bladder or bowel mucosa, or distant spread, according to the staging criteria

blocks.text: The precise subdivisions depend on histological type, depth of invasion, lymphovascular space invasion, molecular characteristics and the presence or location of extrauterine disease.
Do not assign a definitive stage based on endometrial thickness alone.
Treatment is individualised according to stage, histological type and grade, molecular classification, fitness for surgery, fertility wishes and the multidisciplinary team's assessment.

For many patients with operable endometrial cancer, the main treatment is total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, with appropriate nodal assessment depending on risk and tumour characteristics.
Minimally invasive surgery may be appropriate in selected patients.

blocks.title: Depending on risk, pathology and stage, additional treatment may include:

items.text: Combined approaches in selected high-risk disease.

blocks.text: Not every patient requires postoperative radiotherapy or chemotherapy.
Selected patients with carefully defined low-risk endometrioid disease may be considered for fertility-sparing treatment, commonly involving progestogen therapy and close histological surveillance.
This requires specialist counselling because it is not appropriate for every tumour type or stage.

items.text: Hormonal treatment for selected hormone-sensitive tumours.
Immunotherapy or targeted treatment when indicated by tumour characteristics and current guidance.
Genetic counselling when an inherited cancer syndrome is suspected.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. Counselling a patient with confirmed endometrial cancer

blocks.text: Use a structured, compassionate approach.

"The biopsy has shown cancer arising from the lining of the uterus. I appreciate that this may be difficult news to receive. The next step is to review the exact tumour type and grade and determine whether it has spread beyond the uterus.

Many endometrial cancers are diagnosed while still confined to the uterus, when treatment can be effective. We cannot give you an accurate individual prognosis until we have reviewed all the findings. Our specialist team will discuss the treatment options with you, including the benefits, risks and any implications for fertility or hormone function."
Allow the patient to ask questions and offer support. Avoid promising a cure or assigning a stage before the appropriate investigations are completed.
Q1. What is the classic presentation of endometrial cancer?
Postmenopausal bleeding.
Q2. What is the most common histological type?
Endometrioid carcinoma.
Q3. Why does obesity increase the risk?
Adipose aromatase contributes to oestrogen production, while metabolic and hormonal changes can promote endometrial proliferation.
Q4. What is the significance of an endometrial thickness of 12 mm in a woman with postmenopausal bleeding?
It is above the commonly used 4 mm threshold and warrants endometrial assessment, usually including tissue sampling or other appropriate investigation.
Q5. Can a thin endometrium exclude cancer in every patient?
No. Persistent or recurrent bleeding requires further evaluation even if the endometrium is thin.
Q6. What is the role of endometrial biopsy?
It provides tissue for histopathological diagnosis and can identify hyperplasia, EIN and carcinoma.
Q7. What is Lynch syndrome?
An inherited mismatch repair disorder associated with increased risk of colorectal, endometrial and other cancers.
Q8. What is the usual definitive treatment for many operable endometrial cancers?
Total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, with nodal assessment and additional treatment according to risk and staging.
Q9. Is endometrial biopsy required for every woman with postmenopausal bleeding?
The evaluation pathway varies. In selected patients, TVUS may be used initially, but sampling is required when the findings are abnormal, inadequate or when bleeding persists or recurs.
Q10. Why is molecular classification important?
It provides prognostic information and can help guide adjuvant treatment and selected systemic treatment decisions.

items.text: Dismissing postmenopausal bleeding as normal ageing.
Attributing bleeding solely to anticoagulants or hormone therapy.
Using the 4 mm ultrasound threshold inappropriately in premenopausal women.
Assuming a thin endometrium excludes cancer despite persistent bleeding.
Confusing endometrial cancer with cervical cancer.
Giving definitive treatment recommendations without histology and staging.
Ignoring Lynch syndrome and relevant family history.
Forgetting fertility wishes and the possibility of selected fertility-sparing management.
Failing to explain the diagnosis compassionately.
R — Reproductive factors, including nulliparity in relevant contexts.
O — Oestrogen without adequate progesterone opposition.
E — Early menarche or late menopause.
N — No ovulation or chronic anovulation.
A — Assess endometrial thickness on TVUS where appropriate.
P — Pelvic imaging for selected staging questions.
L — Laboratory tests and baseline fitness assessment.
E — Evaluate extent of disease and relevant molecular markers.
Postmenopausal bleeding is the classic symptom.
Obesity and unopposed oestrogen are important risk factors for endometrioid carcinoma.
Endometrial biopsy establishes the tissue diagnosis.
Persistent bleeding requires further assessment even with a thin endometrium.
Treatment depends on histology, stage, molecular risk and patient factors.

blocks.text: Exam practice

A 64-year-old woman presents with a single episode of postmenopausal bleeding. TVUS demonstrates an endometrial thickness of 3 mm. Her bleeding stops, but she returns two months later with another episode.
What is the most appropriate next step?
Reassure her permanently because the endometrium is less than 4 mm.
Repeat ultrasound in five years.
Arrange further endometrial assessment, usually including tissue sampling and/or hysteroscopy as indicated.
Diagnose endometrial cancer without further investigation.
